$$ \rho_{\eta\mid y,e}(t\mid y,e)=\frac{\rho_{y\mid\eta,e}(y\mid t,e)\rho_{\eta}(t)}{\rho_{y\mid e}(y\mid e)}=\frac{\rho_{y\mid\eta,e}(y-e\mid t,0)\rho_{\eta}(t)}{\rho_{y\mid e}(y-e\mid 0)}=\rho_{\eta\mid y,e}(t\mid y-e,0). $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}[\theta\mid Y=y]= \displaystyle\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y=y] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\int t\,\rho_{\eta\mid y,e}(t\mid y,e^{*})\,dt \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\int t\,\rho_{\eta\mid y,e}(t\mid y-e^{*},0)\,dt \displaystyle= \displaystyle\ \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\mathbb{E}^{0}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y=y-e^{*}]. $$

Under the measure corresponding to $e=0,$ the variable $Y$ is equal to $Y^{0}$ almost surely. So

$$ \mathbb{E}^{0}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y=y-e^{*}]=\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}=y-e^{*}]. $$

Now,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{e}\left[\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}[\theta\mid Y]\right]=\  \displaystyle\int dy\,\rho_{y\mid e}(y\mid e)\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}[\theta\mid Y=y] \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\int dy\,\rho_{y\mid e}(y\mid e)\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}=y-e^{*}]\right) \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\int dy\,\rho_{y\mid e}(y-e\mid 0)\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}=y-e^{*}]\right), $$

$$ \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial e}\mathbb{E}^{e}\left[\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}[\theta\mid Y]\right]\right|_{e=e^{*}}=\int dy^{\prime}\,\rho_{y\mid e}(y^{\prime}\mid 0)\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}]\right|_{Y^{0}=y^{\prime}}. $$

Recall that $Y=Y^{0}$ conditional on $e=0,$ so $\rho_{y\mid e}(y^{\prime}\mid 0)$ is the density of $Y^{0}$ . The rhs of the previous expression may therefore be written

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]+\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0},\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\int dF_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y)\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle y-\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}-\int dF_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y)\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Lemma D.3 directly implies that

$$ \int dF_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y)\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] $$

is weakly increasing in $y$ , so (D.2) is weakly decreasing in $y$ .

Following the same logic as in the attributes case, monotonicity of (D.2) implies that

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\varepsilon_{k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right], $$

and it follows that

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}\leq\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Thus the marginal value of effort in each subpopulation in the baseline is weakly lower than the expected marginal value of effort when the circumstance $k^{\prime}$ is additionally measured.

### D.3 Proofs of Theorems 2 and B.2

We prove Theorem B.2, from which Theorem 2 follows immediately as a corollary.

#### D.3.1 Part (a)

Fix a baseline family of measured covariates $(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})$ . As established in Lemma D.1, the marginal value of effort is

$$ MV(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right], $$

where $Y^{0}\equiv\theta+\varepsilon$ is the baseline value of the outcome after subtracting out the agent’s effort.

Now suppose the market additional observes the additional attribute $j^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{J},$ and let $\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\equiv\mathcal{J}\cup\{j^{\prime}\}.$ Under the expanded family of measured covariates, the marginal value of effort becomes

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right], $$

where, conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ , $MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}$ is a random variable whose value is a function of the realization of $a_{j^{\prime}}.$

The outcome $Y^{0}$ may be decomposed as

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}}+\delta_{\mathcal{K}}, $$

where

$$ \mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}\equiv\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\theta_{j}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\varepsilon_{k} $$

is constant conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ . The residual type component $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ may be further decomposed as

$$ \eta_{\mathcal{J}}=\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}+\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}, $$

where

$$ \bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}\equiv\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}],\quad\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\equiv\theta-\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}]. $$

We may therefore rewrite (D.3) as

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}+\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}+\delta_{\mathcal{K}}. $$

Now, note that

$$ \eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}-\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}]=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\theta_{j^{\prime}}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\theta_{j^{\prime}}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\right]=\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}. $$

Hence $\mathcal{J}$ -Strong Homoskedasticity of attribute $j^{\prime}$ is equivalent to the assumption that $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is independent of $a_{j^{\prime}}$ conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}).$ Therefore under $\mathcal{J}$ -Strong Homoskedasticity, $Y^{0}$ depends on $a_{j^{\prime}}$ only through $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}.$ It follows that under $\mathcal{J}$ -Strong Homoskedasticity, $\mathbb{E}[\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]=\mathbb{E}[\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]$ , and the latter expectation depends on $a_{j^{\prime}}$ only through $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ .

Using this fact, we may write

$$ \mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]=\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}+\mathbb{E}[\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] $$

and

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ \bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right]. $$

The theorem holds if can we show that the conditional expectation of $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is less responsive to the realization of the outcome $Y$ than the conditional expectation of the original residual $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ . Note that $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ is the sum of the (conditionally) independent variables $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ and $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ , so uncertainty about $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is mechanically lower than uncertainty about $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ . But this does not directly translate into a statement that the posterior expectation of $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is less sensitive to the realization of $Y$ . In general, we are not even guaranteed that higher realizations of $Y$ lead to higher inferences about $\Delta\theta_{\mathcal{J}}$ once we have conditioned on the realization of $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ .2828 28 Recall that our admissibility assumptions are imposed on the original type component $\theta_{j^{\prime}}$ , and not on the constructed $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ . We next prove a key technical lemma, which will imply an analogue of admissibility for our transformed environment.

#### Lemma D.4.

$(\eta_{\mathcal{J}},\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},Y^{0})$ are affiliated conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}).$

#### Proof.

Fix a set of realizations of $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}),$ and condition all distributions on these values. To economize on notation, we suppress explicit conditioning on these covariates throughout this proof. Let $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta,\theta,Y}(u,t,y)$ be the conditional joint density of $(\eta_{\mathcal{J}},\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}},Y^{0})$ . We will show that $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta,\theta,Y}$ is log-supermodular.

Use $\tilde{\rho}_{\theta}(t)$ to denote the density of $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ , $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)$ to denote the conditional density of $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ , and $\tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}(y\mid u)$ to denote the conditional density of $Y^{0}\mid\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ . Note that $Y^{0}$ is independent of $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ conditional on $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ . So $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta,\theta,Y}$ may be decomposed as

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{\eta,\theta,Y}(u,t,y)=\tilde{\rho}_{\theta}(t)\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)\tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}(y\mid u). $$

It is therefore sufficient to show that $\tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}$ and $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}$ are log-supermodular.

First consider $\tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}$ . Decompose $Y^{0}$ as

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}}+\delta_{\mathcal{K}}. $$

Let $\rho_{\delta}(z)$ be the density of $\delta_{\mathcal{K}}$ . Then

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}(y\mid u)=\rho_{\delta}(y-\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}-u). $$

Under Assumption B.1, $\rho_{\delta}$ is log-concave, meaning $\tilde{\rho}_{Y\mid\eta}$ is log-supermodular.

As for $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}$ , let $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta^{\prime}}(w)$ be the density of $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ . Decompose $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ as

$$ \eta_{\mathcal{J}}=\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}+\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}, $$

and recall that if $j^{\prime}$ is $\mathcal{J}$ -Strongly Homoskedastic, then $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is independent of $a_{j^{\prime}}$ and hence $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ . It follows that

$$ \tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)=\tilde{\rho}_{\eta^{\prime}}(u-t), $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u\partial t}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)=-\left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial w^{2}}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta^{\prime}}(w)\right|_{w=u-t}=-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u^{2}}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t). $$

Now, let $\rho_{\eta\mid a}(u\mid\alpha)$ denote the conditional density of $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid a_{j^{\prime}}$ . Define

$$ \zeta(\alpha)\equiv f^{j^{\prime}}(\alpha)+\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid a_{j^{\prime}}=\alpha], $$

so that

$$ \eta_{\mathcal{J}}=\zeta(a_{j^{\prime}})+\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}. $$

Strong Homoskedasticity implies that

$$ \rho_{\eta\mid a}(u\mid\alpha)=\tilde{\rho}_{\eta^{\prime}}(u-\zeta(\alpha))=\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid\zeta(\alpha)). $$

Let $\tilde{\Theta}\equiv\{t\ :\ \zeta(\alpha)=t\text{ for some }\alpha\in A_{j^{\prime}}\}$ denote the support of $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}.$ Fix any $t\in\tilde{\Theta}.$ Then for all $u$ and every $\alpha\in A_{j^{\prime}}$ such that $\zeta(\alpha)=t,$

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u^{2}}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u^{2}}\log\rho_{\eta\mid a}(u\mid\alpha). $$

Let $\rho_{\eta^{\prime}\mid a}$ denote the conditional density of $\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}\mid a_{j^{\prime}}$ . Then $\rho_{\eta\mid a}(u\mid\alpha)=\rho_{\eta^{\prime}\mid a}(u-f^{j^{\prime}}(\alpha)\mid\alpha),$ so that

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u^{2}}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)=\left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial w^{2}}\log\rho_{\eta^{\prime}\mid a}(w\mid\alpha)\right|_{w=u-f^{j^{\prime}}(\alpha)}. $$

Under Assumption B.1, $\rho_{\eta^{\prime}\mid a}$ is log-concave and this final derivative is non-positive, meaning

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u\partial t}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)=-\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u^{2}}\log\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}(u\mid t)\geq 0 $$

for every $u$ and $t\in\tilde{\Theta}.$ Hence $\tilde{\rho}_{\eta\mid\theta}$ is log-supermodular, as desired. ∎

Following arguments identical to those used for the proof of Theorem B.1 (with $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ and $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ playing the roles of $\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ and $\theta_{j^{\prime}}$ ), Lemma D.4 implies

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}\geq\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Thus the marginal value of effort in each subpopulation in the baseline setting is weakly higher than the expected marginal value once attribute $j^{\prime}$ is additionally measured, for any realizations of $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ .

To complete the proof, we must establish that monotonicity holds uniformly across realizations of $a_{j^{\prime}}$ , and not just on average. This follows immediately from the fact that $MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}$ is independent of $a_{j^{\prime}}$ conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ . To see this, decompose $Y$ as

$$ Y=e+\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}+\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}+\delta_{\mathcal{K}}. $$

Strong Homoskedasticity implies that $\Delta\eta_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}$ is independent of $a_{j^{\prime}}$ conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ . Hence $a_{j^{\prime}}$ enters the market’s inference problem only via a known additive shift $\bar{\eta}_{\mathcal{J}\mid j^{\prime}}$ to the agent’s type distribution, and therefore its value does not impact incentives for effort. So these incentives must be independent of $a_{j^{\prime}},$ as claimed.

#### D.3.2 Part (b)

Suppose the market observes the additional circumstance $k^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{K}.$ Let $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}\equiv\mathcal{K}\cup\{k^{\prime}\}.$ Under the expanded family of measured covariates, the marginal value of effort is

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}]\ \middle|\ a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\right]. $$

Define

$$ \bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}\equiv\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid c_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}],\quad\Delta\delta_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\equiv\varepsilon-\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid c_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}]. $$

Then $Y^{0}$ may be decomposed as

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}}+\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}+\Delta\delta_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}. $$

Under Strong Homoskedasticity, $\Delta\delta_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}$ is independent of $c_{k^{\prime}}$ conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}),$ and so the distribution of $Y^{0}$ depends on $c_{k^{\prime}}$ only through $\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}.$ Thus

$$ \mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}]=\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}], $$

and the latter random variable depends on $c_{k^{\prime}}$ only through $\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}.$ Therefore, in a manner analogous to the attribute case, the marginal value of effort after measuring $j^{\prime}$ depends on $c_{k^{\prime}}$ only through $\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}$ and may be written

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ \bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right]. $$

#### Lemma D.5.

$(\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},\delta_{\mathcal{K}},Y^{0})$ are affiliated conditional on $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ .

#### Proof.

This proof follows along very similar lines to the proof of Lemma D.4. Fix realizations of $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}),$ condition all distributions on their values, and suppress explicit conditioning on these covariates. Let $\rho_{\eta}(u)$ be the conditional density of $\eta_{\mathcal{J}}$ and $\rho_{\delta^{\prime}\mid c}(x\mid z)$ be the conditional density of $\delta_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\mid c_{k^{\prime}}$ . The conditions required for the steps of the proof of Lemma D.4 to go through are that $\rho_{\eta}(u)$ is log-concave, $\rho_{\delta^{\prime}\mid c}(x\mid z)$ is log-concave in $x$ for all $z,$ and $\Delta\delta_{\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}$ is independent of $\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K}\mid k^{\prime}}$ . The first two properties are ensured by Assumption B.1, while the final property holds under Strong Homoskedasticity. ∎

We compare $MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}$ and $MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}$ in a manner very similar to the attribute case. Fix realizations of $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}).$ Define

$$ \widetilde{F}_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y)\equiv\Pr(\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}\leq z\mid Y^{0}=y,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}) $$

to be the distribution function of $\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}$ conditional on the outcome $Y^{0}$ .

Decompose $Y^{0}$ as

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\eta_{\mathcal{J}}+\delta_{\mathcal{K}}. $$

Taking expectations of each side conditional on $(Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}})$ yields

$$ Y^{0}=\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}+\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]+\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\int d\widetilde{F}_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y^{\prime})\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle y-\mu_{(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K})}-\int d\widetilde{F}_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y^{\prime})\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Lemma D.5 directly implies that

$$ \int d\widetilde{F}_{\varepsilon}(z\mid y)\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\mathcal{K}}\mid Y^{0}=y,\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}}=z,a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] $$

is nondecreasing in $y$ , so (D.4) is nonincreasing in $y$ .

Following the same logic as in the attributes case, monotonicity of (D.4) implies that

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial Y^{0}}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{\mathcal{J}}\mid Y^{0},\bar{\delta}_{\mathcal{K},k^{\prime}},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\ \middle|\ Y^{0},a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right], $$

and it follows that

$$ MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}\leq\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]. $$

Thus the marginal value of effort in each subpopulation in the baseline is weakly lower than the expected marginal value of effort when the circumstance $k^{\prime}$ is additionally measured.

The final step in the proof is to establish that monotonicity holds uniformly across realizations of the additional circumstance, and not just on average. This follows from nearly identical work to the argument for the attributes case.

### D.4 Proof of Theorem 3

Define $\delta\equiv\beta/(1-\beta).$ Then equilibrium effort under any measured covariates can be written as $e^{*}_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}=\delta\cdot MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}.$ We will characterize the aggregate welfare change from measuring a new covariate as a function of $\delta$ , which can be mapped onto an equivalent characterization in terms of $\beta.$

Consider first the case in which the market observes the new attribute $j^{\prime}.$ Let $\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\equiv\mathcal{J}\cup\{j^{\prime}\}.$ The aggregate change in welfare from measuring $j^{\prime},$ as a function of $\delta,$ is

$$ \Delta\overline{W}(\delta)=\mathbb{E}\left[w_{0}(\delta\cdot MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}})-w_{0}(\delta\cdot MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}})\right], $$

where

$$ w_{0}(e)\equiv e-\frac{1}{2}e^{2}. $$

The aggregate change in welfare is a quadratic function of $\delta,$ whose first derivative is

$$ \frac{d}{d\delta}\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)=\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}\right]-\delta\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right]. $$

Observe that $\overline{W}(0)=0$ and

$$ \left.\frac{d}{d\delta}\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\right|_{\delta=0}=\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}\right]\leq 0 $$

with the inequality implied by regularity of $j^{\prime}$ . So $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)$ is a quadratic function that vanishes at $\delta=0$ and is nonincreasing there. Suppose first that $j^{\prime}$ is strictly regular, so that $\Delta\overline{W}$ is strictly decreasing at 0. Then its shape must then satisfy either of:

- • $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)$ is strictly convex and intersects zero exactly once for $\delta>0,$

- • $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)$ is weakly concave and does not intersect zero for any $\delta>0.$

Define $\delta^{*}\equiv\inf\{\delta>0\ :\ \Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\geq 0\}$ . This threshold lies in $(0,\infty),$ and has the property that $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)>0$ for $\delta>\delta^{*},$ and $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\leq 0$ for $\delta\in(0,\delta^{*}]$ . Further, $\delta^{*}<\infty$ if and only if $\Delta\overline{W}$ is strictly convex. Convexity is determined by the sign of

$$ \frac{d^{2}}{d\delta^{2}}\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)=\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}-MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right]. $$

Hence $\delta^{*}<\infty$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right]>\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right].$ Letting $\beta^{*}\equiv\delta^{*}/(1+\delta^{*})$ therefore yields a reputation weight threshold with the desired properties.

On the other hand, suppose that $j^{\prime}$ is weakly but not strictly regular. Write

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}] \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}-\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}])^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]+\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]^{2} \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\text{Var}\left(MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right)+\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]^{2}. $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2} \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]^{2}-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}+\text{Var}\left(MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right). $$

Weak but not strict regularity implies that $MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}=\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]$ with probability 1, so that

$$ \mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}=\text{Var}\left(MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right)\geq 0 $$

with probability 1. Therefore $\Delta\overline{W}$ is at least weakly concave. Weak but not strict regularity additionally implies that $\Delta\overline{W}$ has zero slope at $\delta=0.$ Hence in this case $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\leq 0$ for all $\delta>0$ , in which case $\delta^{*}=\infty$ and $\beta^{*}=\infty.$ We may summarize the work for the strictly and weakly regular cases by the result that $\beta^{*}<\infty$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right]>\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J}^{\prime},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right]$ . Indeed, in the strictly regular case, this equivalence was directly established, while in the weakly regular case, it is true both that $\beta^{*}=\infty$ and that the latter inequality cannot hold.

Now suppose the market observes the new circumstance $k^{\prime}.$ Calculations very similar to those for the attribute case show that $\Delta\overline{W}$ is a quadratic function of $\delta$ which vanishes at $\delta=0$ and is weakly increasing there, and strictly increasing if $k^{\prime}$ is strictly regular. It is concave iff $\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}^{2}\right]\geq\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right],$ with the concavity strict iff the inequality is.

If $k^{\prime}$ is only weakly regular, then the calculations for the attribute case show that $\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}^{2}\right]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}\right],$ meaning that $\Delta\overline{W}$ must be at least weakly concave, in which case $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\leq 0$ for all $\delta>0.$ In this case we set $\delta_{*}=0$ and $\beta_{*}=\delta_{*}/(1+\delta_{*})=0.$

Going forward, suppose that $k^{\prime}$ is strictly regular. Defining $\delta_{*}\equiv\inf\{\delta>0\ :\ \Delta\overline{W}(\delta)\leq 0\}$ yields a threshold in $(0,\infty]$ with the property that $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)<0$ for all $\delta>\delta_{*}$ and $\Delta\overline{W}(\delta)>0$ for all $\delta\in(0,\delta_{*}).$ This threshold is finite iff $\Delta\overline{W}$ is strictly concave function. Calculations very similar to the attribute case imply that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2} \displaystyle=\  \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]^{2}-MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}+\text{Var}\left(MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}\right). $$

Strict regularity implies that the difference of the first two terms on the rhs is non-negative for every realization of $(a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}),$ and positive with positive probability. Further, the conditional variance of $MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}$ must be non-negative. Therefore

$$ \mathbb{E}[MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}^{\prime}}^{2}\mid a_{\mathcal{J}},c_{\mathcal{K}}]\geq MV_{\mathcal{J},\mathcal{K}}^{2}, $$

with the inequality strict with positive probability. Taking the unconditional expectation of both sides yields the desired strict concavity of $\Delta\overline{W},$ implying $\delta_{*}<\infty.$ Letting $\beta_{*}\equiv\delta_{*}/(1+\delta_{*})$ yields a reputation weight with the desired properties.

### D.5 Proof of Proposition 1

We prove the first part of the result, with the second following from nearly identical arguments. To streamline notation, throughout this proof we will drop superscripts on $Y^{0}$ and $\bar{Y}^{0}.$

Under Assumption 3, conditioning on the value of $X$ is equivalent to conditioning on the value of $\bar{Y}.$ The desired result can therefore be established using a technique very similar to the proof of Theorem B.1(a) subsequent to Lemma D.2, with $\bar{Y}$ playing the role of $\theta_{j^{\prime}}$ . That argument requires two conditions: A) $(\bar{Y},Y)$ are statistically affiliated, and B) $(\bar{Y},\theta)$ are statistically affiliated conditional on $Y.$ We maintain condition A by hypothesis, so it remains only to establish condition B.

Let $\rho_{Y\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y\mid y^{\prime},t)$ be the conditional density of $Y$ given $(\bar{Y},\theta)$ ; $\rho_{\bar{Y},\theta}$ be the joint density of $(\bar{Y},\theta);$ and $\rho_{Y}$ be the marginal density of $Y.$ Then by Bayes’ rule,

$$ \rho_{\bar{Y},\theta\mid Y}(y^{\prime},t\mid y)=\frac{\rho_{Y\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y\mid y^{\prime},t)\rho_{\bar{Y},\theta}(y^{\prime},t)}{\rho_{Y}(y)}. $$

Because $(\bar{Y},\theta)$ are affiliated, the density $\rho_{\bar{Y},\theta}$ is log-supermodular. To establish condition B, it is therefore sufficient to show that $\rho_{Y\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y\mid y^{\prime},t)$ is log-supermodular in $(y^{\prime},t),$ holding $y$ fixed.

Let $\rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(e\mid y^{\prime},t)$ and $\rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y}}(e\mid y^{\prime})$ be the conditional densities of $\varepsilon$ given $(\bar{Y},\theta)$ and $\bar{Y},$ respectively. Given the conditional independence of $\theta$ and $\varepsilon$ given $X$ and the invertibility of $\mathbb{E}(\bar{Y}\mid X),$ it follows that $\theta$ and $\varepsilon$ are independent conditional on $\bar{Y}.$ Therefore

$$ \rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(e\mid y^{\prime},t)=\rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y}}(e\mid y^{\prime}) $$

for all $t,$ allowing us to write

$$ \rho_{Y\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y\mid y^{\prime},t)=\rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y-t\mid y^{\prime},t)=\rho_{\varepsilon\mid\bar{Y}}(y-t\mid y^{\prime}). $$

Let $\rho_{\varepsilon,\bar{Y}}(e,y^{\prime})$ be the joint density of $(\varepsilon,\bar{Y})$ and $\rho_{\bar{Y}}(y^{\prime})$ be the marginal density of $\bar{Y}.$ Then using Bayes’ rule, we have

$$ \rho_{Y\mid\bar{Y},\theta}(y\mid y^{\prime},t)=\frac{\rho_{\varepsilon,\bar{Y}}(y-t,y^{\prime})}{\rho_{\bar{Y}}(y^{\prime})}. $$

Condition B therefore follows if $\rho_{\varepsilon,\bar{Y}}$ is log-submodular. Equivalently, $\rho_{-\varepsilon,\bar{Y}}$ must be log-supermodular, where $\rho_{-\varepsilon,\bar{Y}}$ is the joint density of $(-\varepsilon,\bar{Y}).$ This condition is equivalent to affiliation of $(-\varepsilon,\bar{Y}),$ as hypothesized.

### D.6 Proof of Lemma 1

In a multivariate Gaussian environment the conditional mean of output is

$$ \bar{Y}^{0}=\mu+(b+d)X, $$

satisfying Assumption 3 whenever $b+d\neq 0$ . Since $(X,Z,W)$ are jointly Gaussian and $\bar{Y}^{0}$ and $Y^{0}$ are each linear combinations of $(X,Z,W),$ the pair $(\bar{Y}^{0},Y^{0})$ are also jointly Gaussian. Additionally,

$$ Y^{0}=\bar{Y}^{0}+Z+W, $$

and since $\bar{Y}^{0}$ is independent of $Z+W$ it follows that $Y^{0}$ and $\bar{Y}^{0}$ are positively correlated. Therefore $(\bar{Y}^{0},Y^{0})$ are affiliated, satisfying Assumption 4. Moreover, conditional expectations in multivariate Gaussian environments are linear in the conditioning variable, ensuring that Assumption 5 is satisfied. Finally, mutual independence of $X$ , $Z,$ and $W$ implies that $(\theta,\varepsilon)$ are independent conditional on $X,$ satisfying Assumption 6.

### D.7 Proof of Proposition 2

Prior to the measurement, $(\theta,Y^{0})$ have joint distribution

$$ \left(\begin{array}[]{c}\theta\\
Y^{0}\end{array}\right)\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mu\\
\mu\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sigma_{\theta}^{2}&\sigma_{\theta,Y}\\
\sigma_{\theta,Y}&\sigma_{Y}^{2}\end{array}\right)\right) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{\theta}^{2}=b^{2}\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{z}^{2},\quad\sigma_{\theta,Y}=b(b+d)\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{z}^{2},\quad\sigma_{Y}^{2}=(b+d)^{2}\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{z}^{2}+\sigma_{w}^{2}. $$

The market’s type forecast given equilibrium effort $e^{*}$ is therefore

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{e^{*}}(\theta\mid Y) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid Y^{0}=Y-e^{*})=\mu+\frac{\sigma_{\theta,Y}}{\sigma_{Y}^{2}}\cdot(Y-\mu-e^{*}), $$

implying that the baseline marginal value of effort is

$$ \displaystyle MV=\frac{\sigma_{\theta,Y}}{\sigma_{Y}^{2}}=\frac{b(b+d)\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{z}^{2}}{(b+d)^{2}\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{z}^{2}+\sigma_{w}^{2}}. $$

Meanwhile, after measuring $X$ , the conditional joint distribution of $(\theta,Y^{0})$ is

$$ \left(\begin{array}[]{c}\theta\\
Y^{0}\end{array}\right)\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mu+bX\\
\mu+(b+d)X\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sigma_{z}^{2}&\sigma_{z}^{2}\\
\sigma_{z}^{2}&\sigma_{z}^{2}+\sigma_{w}^{2}\end{array}\right)\right). $$

Given equilibrium effort $e^{**},$ the market’s posterior type forecast after measuring $X$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{e^{**}}(\theta\mid X,Y)=\mathbb{E}(\theta\mid X,Y^{0}=Y-e^{**})=\mu+bX+\frac{\sigma_{z}^{2}}{\sigma_{z}^{2}+\sigma_{w}^{2}}(Y-e^{**}-\mu-(b+d)X). $$

The agent’s marginal value of effort under the expanded dataset is therefore

$$ MV_{+}=\frac{\sigma_{z}^{2}}{\sigma_{z}^{2}+\sigma_{w}^{2}}. $$

Comparing the expressions for $MV$ and $MV_{+}$ just derived yields the identity in the proposition statement.
